speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise and commence today's debate on Bill C-76, the 1992 budget implementation act.
In so doing I note that it is almost one year since that budget came down. As with all budgets, they are debated and approved in principle. The will of Parliament is indeed known following that approval, yet here we are, almost one year later, proceeding with the implementation of the legislative measures that flow from that budget.
It is a sad comment on Parliament and rather indeed more a comment on my hon. friends opposite than on the government that one year later we are still debating it. It is regrettable the government is obliged to use closure to vote through a fairly straightforward measure the fundamental principles of which were approved almost one year ago by this Parliament.
That seems to be what has happened here. It is a sad state and a sad comment on the state of parliamentary
democracy in this country that a government cannot proceed with fairly straightforward basic legislation without the imposition of time allocation and closure.
Nevertheless this government is determined to proceed with necessary restraint measures. It is determined to proceed with deficit control measures, and I might say that possibly, our hon. friends on the other side are finally getting the message.

speechtext:
I do not know. I have listened to their leaders. My hon. colleague for Mississauga South says that he does not think so.
I noticed as recently as yesterday that the leader of the New Democratic Party of Canada has now become a convert. She is for deficit control. We cannot necessarily make sense of it but we have certainly heard the recent pronouncements of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to deficit control.
I suppose at some point in the future we might even look forward to the day when my hon. friends opposite will not just talk about deficit control, they will actually walk into this place and support measures designed to achieve it. We will wait for that and some day we will see it.
I want to say two things in my remarks this morning if I may. As always, I will be very mindful of the clock, Madam Speaker. I will not abuse your patience. You have always been very indulgent of me in terms of the clock.
First I want to talk a little bit about the specifics of this piece of legislation. Then I want to talk about the subject of fiscal restraint and deficit control in general. Since my friends opposite have now become converts to this I would like to assist them in their learning curve of understanding the process by which this government has been making such significant progress over the course of the last eight and a half years.

February 19, 1993
Government Orders
Bill C-76, the budget implementation act, 1992 of course was in the budget. I might say it was a fiscally prudent, socially responsive and economically sound budget.
The budget contained measures to boost the competitiveness of Canadian firms and workers. It is interesting to note that it is having an effect. Canadian competitiveness is up 2 per cent in the past year compared to only a 1.2 per cent increase in our neighbours to the south.
Indeed the budget, the measures and actions of this government notwithstanding the gnashing of teeth from our friends on the other side would seem to be having a significant amount of progress.
As well, the budget brought forward further actions to reduce government expenditures in order that we could ultimately reduce taxes. I would remind all hon. members that last year's budget brought with it tax reduction.
When this government says it is going to bring tax reduction, it does. We had the proof of it in the 1992 budget. The Canadian public will experience that as they fill out their income tax forms this year. They will find that the bite is not great, but a little bit smaller which is at least an improvement over having taxes go up.
There were a number of tax relief measures provided in that budget for Canadian families and indeed for students and Canadians with disabilities. Measures were also part of the government's over-all strategy to promote economic recovery, strengthen Canada's international competitiveness and further control its expenditures.
Bill C-76 initially contained four elements. It contained references to the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Salaries Act, the Lobbyists Registration Act and the Canada Student Loans Act.
Since Bill C-76 was originally tabled, we have had the December economic statement which brought even more generous benefits and benefits that will be very positive incentives for small business in this country.
Due to the diligence of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, that legislation has been brought forward. On this one I must give credit where credit is due. I must compliment my hon. friends opposite for not having held up that bill with respect to the Small Businesses Loans Act. That act is very important to thousands and thousands of small businesses in Canada.
I would like to commend them for working with the government to move that legislation along. It is now at committee stage. We look forward to seeing that legislation back very soon to be passed. Then small businesses from coast to coast in Canada can benefit from that legislation.
That leaves the three remaining elements. The amendments to the Salaries Act reduced the salaries of the Prime Minister and the cabinet ministers by 5 per cent effective April 1, 1992.1 will be interested to see if my hon. friends opposite will be supporting this bill.
To not support this bill would be a clear indication that they believe the salary reductions should not hit the Prime Minister and the cabinet ministers. I assume if they vote against that it is their indication that they feel the Prime Minister and the ministers of this government are doing such an excellent job that they should not have their salaries reduced.
Unfortunately some of them might be beguiled into thinking it is because they hope to be sitting in the treasury benches some time before the next year or two or three should pass. I hate to break the news to them but I say they should look at their vote on this act more from the perspective of endorsing the excellent job being done by the incumbents on those benches right now.
Nevertheless this government believes in leading by example: do as I do, not as I say. That is why the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Forestry who I see here this morning and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans along with others who are here, lead by example. Restraint starts with restraining oneself. That is a very commendable decision and a commendable example taken by these measures.
The Minister of Finance in bringing forward his budget also indicated the government would strengthen its cost recovery performance. One area we believe should operate on a cost recovery basis of course is lobbyist registration. We know the Lobbyists Registration Act is of great interest to members of this House.
February 19, 1993

There indeed is to be a fee imposed on lobbyists to cover the cost of that process. User pay of course is a concept that has underlined many of the policies of this government. Many people come before members of Parliament requesting that more money be spent, but the fact of the matter is in order for government to spend money, somebody has to pay. I do not hear indications of support very often from my friends opposite or anywhere else that they favour tax increases.
If there is not a user pay concept where it makes sense such as in a case of lobbyists who are obviously in the business to make money, it is only appropriate that the cost of providing that service be raised. I should point out that as is the practice with this government there will be full consultation with the constituency affected by this decision before it is raised. Concern was raised at the committee looking at lobbyist registration.
Some people or groups, for example student organizations or poverty groups, might be penalized by this measure because they lack the financial means to pay the registration fee to register as lobbyists. Quite simply, these people are not required to register as lobbyists unless they are permanently employed and are employed as lobbyists, permanent representatives making continual representations over the years to the government. In other words, a professional lobbyist. There is a difference between advocacy and lobbying and that is recognized and of course it is the responsibility of the lobbyist to recognize it.
With regard to the Canada Student Loans Act the amendments in Bill C-76 deal essentially with three major items: removing the six-month, post-school, interest free period as of the 1993-1994 loan year; updating the alternative payment formula for provinces choosing to opt out of the program in the future, including an increase to the period of notice for such action; and making the administration of the program easier by allowing the minister to prescribe the forms to be used.
These measures will remove the interest subsidy during the six-month period after borrowers have completed their studies when they are generally in a position to assume responsibility for repayment. Aside from

self-enrichment, one of the reasons for further education is to provide and prepare oneself for employment in the work place. Notwithstanding the gnashing of teeth I hear day after day from some of my colleagues opposite, it is interesting to note that Canada in fact has the best record of job creation in the G-7. So this makes eminent sense.

In any event these measures will-

My hon. friend asked me to drop some more. There is so much wisdom here, I would not want to lose any of it because I know how much you are looking forward to hearing it all.
These measures will remove the interest subsidy during the six-month period after borrowers have completed their studies when they are generally in a position to assume responsibility for repayment. They will update an obsolete alternative payment formula to ensure that the cost of previously authorized loans in a province would be deducted from any future alternative payments. They will streamline the program as well.
It is interesting to note that since its inception in 1964 the Canada Student Loans Program has enabled more than 2.5 million students to pursue post-secondary studies thus contributing to the development of a well-educated and adaptable work force.
I bet a show of hands in this House would indicate that there are members present who over the years have benefited from that program.
Indeed an additional $100 million in Canada student loans was provided to needy students in 1991-92. This represents an increase of 16 per cent in assistance available under the program.
Notwithstanding the continued importance of the Canada Student Loans Program in maintaining an accessible post-secondary learning system, it is necessary to modernize the program to ensure its continued ability to provide assistance to needy students.

Government Orders
The amendments proposed in Bill C-76 should therefore be viewed in the context of other measures currently being undertaken by the government to strengthen and improve the Canada Student Loans Program.
The February 1992 budget signalled the government's intention to reform the program and this was reiterated in the December economic statement. The government undertook to initiate negotiations with lenders on a new financing structure for the program. The objective is to reduce the high default costs and improve the over-all efficiency of the program. Lender risk sharing, a new rate structure and administrative streamlining are among the anticipated outcomes of the new financing arrangements.
In addition, by reducing default costs and improving program efficiency, it will be possible to enhance assistance for needy students. Specifically, financial restructuring is expected to provide the scope to eliminate the 3 per cent guarantee fee on new loans and to increase aid to needy students, once again showing that this government listens. When that 3 per cent fee was introduced it was criticized roundly by my friends opposite. I am sure they will stand in their places today and commend the government for having heard what they and others have said in responding in this way.
I would like to emphasize that under the new financing arrangements the government will continue to ensure that needy students have access to financial assistance so they can pursue post-secondary studies. This was the purpose for which the program was created and will remain so under the new arrangements. The legislative amendments required to establish the new financing arrangements are expected to be introduced shortly.
I want to talk about some concerns that were raised in committee about the Canada Student Loans Program. In particular, members were concerned about two related issues; the rising student debt loads and increased bankruptcies.
With respect to the rising debt load of students, while the debt load of final year students has risen over the past five years, less than 5 per cent of Canada's student loan recipients had debts of over $15,000. About 85 per cent of the borrowers have less than $10,000 in loans. Those with higher debts are university students with the best prospects for high employment rates and incomes.
In fact, most of the borrowers who default have loans of less than $15,000. Having said that, let me assure the House that the Secretary of State's officials will continue to follow the situation closely.
A related concern is the higher bankruptcy rate associated with higher student debt load. There has been a substantial increase in bankruptcies involving student loans, but for the most part this is the result of the weak economy over the past two years, with which we are all familiar. As well, with increasing numbers of mature students receiving loans, we are starting to see greater numbers of bankruptcies in which student loans are a relatively small portion of the debt.
The Canada Student Loans Program has served the countiy well during its 28 years. It has provided $7.6 billion worth of assistance to over 2.5 million Canadians, allowing them to pursue their studies at thousands of designated institutions. However, the government has recognized the need to modernize the program, to improve its effectiveness in providing learning opportunities. It is clear that the proposals for the program's modernization will ensure that it better serves the needs of present and future generations of students. Canada as a whole will benefit.
I want to speak briefly about the business of debt and debt reduction in general, because that is what this legislation is all about. It is about debt reduction and deficit reduction.
Federal debt piled up rapidly in comparison to the gross domestic product in the mid-seventies and the early eighties as structural imbalances developed between expenditures and revenues. I think it is important to understand this.
I noticed in following the debates that earlier this week the Minister of Finance made the comment that this government, in eight and a half years in office, has not added a single, not one penny-I believe he said a red penny, I have never seen a red penny-but not a penny to the national debt. It is true. On the other hand, the finance critic for the Liberal Party said: "But the debt has doubled since the Tories have been in power".
A reasonable Canadian might ask: who is telling the truth? It is very simple. They are both telling the truth. I think it is important that this business of debt be explained so that people can understand it. There are
February 19, 1993

three concepts: the concept of debt, the concept of deficit and the concept of surplus.
A deficit quite simply is spending more money than you are taking in. For example, when this government came into office in September 1984 it inherited a situation where the previous government was spending $1.33 for every dollar it was taking in. That 33 cents is a deficit.
A surplus is if you are spending less than you are taking in, which is what this government is doing today. In fact in the most recent year, notwithstanding the recession, the government saved Canadian taxpayers over $6 billion in spending on programs, $6 billion less than it was taking in. That is what a surplus is.
If you take the 33 cents more that was being spent than the dollar that was being taken in, once spent, it accumulates and is called debt. Debt is an accumulated thing.
If you have a credit card, it is great, you do not have to worry about what you are spending. If I want to spend money I spend until my pocket is empty, but if I have a credit card I can keep spending. I do not have any money any more.
By spending monthly more than I take in, I start accumulating a debt. Eventually I have to pay that debt off but there is a problem because as long as that debt is there it accrues interest.
We put money in the bank but we expect the bank to pay us interest on the money because what we put in the bank is a loan to the bank. The same thing applies in reverse. If I am borrowing money by using a credit card, the bank expects me to pay interest on it. The same thing applies to government.
It is interesting to note that when this government came into power in September 1984 the previous government of the day-that $1.33 I spoke of a minute ago-was running a deficit of $16 billion a year on its expenditures. Meanwhile that had accumulated a debt of $206 billion.
On the day this government came into office there was a deficit on actually running the government of $16 billion more than was being taken in. There was a $206 billion debt already accumulated on which in that year alone the interest payments were $22 billion.

Guess what? You have to add the $16 billion operating deficit, together with the $22 billion of debt that was accumulated in that year, and that is why when this government came into office there was a $38 billion deficit on the over-all accounts of the government.
What has the government done? The government had a different approach. It believed a business cannot be run that way and government is a business. It believed that debt had to be brought into line. The government has gradually brought that situation into line by reducing expenditures.
It is interesting to note that since it came into office, the government has reduced expenditures, compared with what its predecessor was doing, by an accumulative total of $118 billion. That is equivalent to all the money that was spent running the government this year.
The first year the government managed to cut spending down by $4.8 billion, then $7.9 billion, $9.4 billion, $11.3 billion, $14.2 billion, $20.2 billion, $23.3 billion and this most recent fiscal year, it reduced spending from what it would have been on the Liberal track of $26.9 billion. That is pretty significant.
What would have happened if the deficit control measures of this government had not been brought into line? Where would we be today? The $38.5 billion deficit which was the legacy of that Liberal government, without the restraint measures that this government had brought in, today would be, imagine this, $82.5 billion. The deficit would be $82.5 billion today. I do not even know if there is a computer that could add up what the debt would be in that circumstance. Of course the government has been bringing that deficit down. It is very difficult to bring it all down in one snap move. It takes time to bring it down. This government gradually reduced that debt through deficit reduction programs.
The $206 billion legacy, Mr. Trudeau's legacy to Canadians, with compound interest of $237 billion added to it would have totalled $443 billion. That is what the debt would be if we compounded Mr. Trudeau's legacy to Canadians. By operating since 1987 in the black, by operating with a surplus, the government has prevented the growth of that debt to the point that it is more in the vicinity of $420 billion today. It is still an outrageous sum.

February 19, 1993

It will take generations to pay off, but at least it is now under control.
I hear a lot of scoffing from the other side about what I am saying even though they know every word of it is true. The government has brought in many measures to control the debt. It is interesting to note that every one of these measures has been opposed by the newest disciples of debt reduction: our friends opposite both in the Liberal Party and in the New Democratic Party who are now converts to deficit control. We brought in measures to reduce the rate of growth of transfers to the provinces. They say: "Oh, shameful". They call that off-loading. The provinces spend money and the federal government is supposed to subsidize them whether or not it is out of control.
When we brought in Bill C-32, the Canada Assistance Plan Act, and BUI C-60, Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements, members on the other side were opposed. The government has brought in measures to streamline the operations of government. There have been six pieces of legislation since I have been here: the Budget Implementation Act, 1991; the Debt Servicing and Reduction Account Act; the Spending Control Act; the dissolutions act; and the Government expenditure restraint act, 1990. Indeed we have the Budget Implementation Act before committee right now, BUI C-93. Every one of those was opposed by those people over there. We try to streamline government because we believe that leaner government can be as efficient as fatter government sometimes. Yet they oppose it.
We have privatized Crown corporations. There is a belief on the other side that whenever something is created in the way of a government body or agency it is supposed to be there forever. We believe that an agency, a council, a board, a commission or a department is created because there is a need for it. Once the need has been fulfUIed we do not keep that bureaucracy and keep paying for it. If there is a better way to do it, if we can amalgamate, streamline and provide as efficient or maybe even a more efficient service to the public, then we do so. If the problem can be handled in the private sector our phUosophy is that the government should get out of it altogether.
We have privatized a number of Crown corporations and every one was opposed by my friends on the other side. We brought in measures to restrain the salaries of
public officials from the Prime Minister on down, as I said earlier and as is in this piece of legislation: the public service employment act, pension benefits act, budget implementation act and the government restraint act. Every one of these was opposed across the aisle.
We have restrained grants and contributions. We have reduced budgets by 10 per cent across the board. It is painful. Nobody likes to have their budget cut back. Frequently I have said, as have my colleagues, that when witnesses have appeared before us in committee they have said: "Don't cut this program; this program is important". Every program is important in the eyes of somebody. So to come before government and say "gore somebody else's ox, don't gore mine", just does not work.
Fair, responsible and competent government is government that tries to live within the means available to it. That means having the courage and the integrity, I might say, to bring together restraint when restraint is necessary.
What has been the results? The results are impressive. Everybody knows that we have been through a serious recession throughout the world for the last couple of years. It has hurt a lot of people. It has hurt people in this country. It has hurt people in my South Shore riding. It has hurt people all over the world.
My friends opposite would like to take a simplistic approach, assume the ignorance of the public and blame it all on the free trade agreement, the GST or something like that. However, if we look at the performance of our country compared to other countries during this difficult time, we find that the record is pretty impressive.
If we remove the inflationary effect and look at program expenditure growth in Canada, the record between 1984 and 1990 was .1 of a per cent while in every other G-7 country it was higher: 1.8 per cent in the U.S.,
2.5	per cent in the U.K., right up to 4 per cent in Italy.
As I mentioned earlier, productivity is going up in Canada. In 1992 it was up by 2 per cent compared to 1.2 per cent in the United States. That is not a bad record.
Turning to job creation in Canada, we hear moaning and groaning about the free trade agreement and how we should all be afraid of the Mexicans because the NAFTA is coming. Let us take a look at the record. Canada has the best job creation record in the G-7:12.9 per cent compared with 11.3 per cent in the U.S., 10.5
February 19, 1993

per cent in Japan, all the way down to 3.6 per cent in France. Our situation is not bad at all.
What is the alternative? We will have an election this year. Canadians are mad at governments. Generally speaking if governments take tough, responsible decisions they become unpopular. There is nothing that focuses the mind like the issuance of a writ, as I have heard the Prime Minister say on a number of occasions.
The minute that writ drops it is no longer: "How do you feel about the government", but "who do you want to trust the future of your country to? Who do you feel has the competence to handle what is going on?" There is no doubt in my mind about which way Canadians will go when the election comes. They are going to pick a Prime Minister and a government that have laid it on the line and have said: "These are the realities. We need the courage to face them". They are not going to pick an alternative.
We know where the New Democratic Party is coming from. It has presented its economic plan. We have seen its economic approach have an absolutely devastating effect on the province of Ontario in the last couple of years. We are also beginning to see the impact in places like British Columbia.
I noticed the Leader of the New Democratic Party yesterday came out with her economic policy document: A Strategy for Full Employment. I reviewed this document last night and I found it interesting that she said her strategy for new employment will eventually lead to
1.601.000	new jobs by 1998. That is in her plan. Her plan will involve spending more money.
It says in the document that the objective of the NDP is to contain the deficit over the next parliamentary term but not to reduce it. It is planning to increase taxes and increase spending. As a result the bottom line is looser money and fiscal policy, and a significantly higher tax burden on Canadians is projected, all to create
1.601.0000	new jobs, full employment by 1998.
Yet, if we look at the analysis of the Conference Board of Canada just following the same track we have been following, the one that has been opposed so thoroughly by the New Democratic Party, and getting the deficit under control, what will be the result? We must remem-

ber that NDP figure of 1,601,000 new jobs. The Conference Board says the government's approach will result in: 1,651,000 jobs or 50,000 more new jobs. This means there will be 50,000 more jobs plus deficit and debt control as well, as opposed to allowing it to mushroom.
I do not think anybody will be fooled by the recent conversion of the New Democratic Party to deficit control. It would have been better to have stayed on the track it was on. At least it was given points for integrity even if its policies were not taken seriously by anybody with a bit of an understanding of economics.
Then we come to our friends across the aisle, the government in waiting, as they see themselves. When the election comes the Canadian people are going to have to look at the Leader of the Opposition and at the Prime Minister. The Liberals think that the Prime Minister has been unpopular and Canadians say they do not like him. Canadians may not like the Prime Minister, I do not know why because I think he is a great guy, but that is fine, they do not have to like somebody to recognize his or her competence. Deep down Canadians know that this Prime Minister has the courage to provide leadership for this country, as he has done for eight and a half years.
When Canadians look across the aisle they say: "Where do the Liberals stand?" Where did they stand when the United Nations and Canada went to war? Where have they stood when they say they want to get the deficit under control? Where have they stood on every single measure that has been brought before this House to control expenditures and reduce the deficit in this country? They have stood against those measures. We can look at the list of items that have been brought forward for expenditures with no indication whatsoever of where the money would come from.
Finally, we see the new economics of the Leader of the Opposition and his party with his recent statement that he is going to abolish the GST. That is $15 billion. He is going to abolish it and only if Canadians elect him will they get to find out where the money is going to come from.

Do not take it from me. Some might not consider me an objective observer of this. Listen to what The Ottawa Sun has to say about Liberal Party economic policy. I quote from the Ottawa Sun on February 4 of this month: "Jean Chretien has come up with his own Liberal brand of voodoo economics by promising taxpayers that a future Liberal government would wave a magic wand and make the nasty old GST disappear. The Liberals would actually replace the unpopular tax with a brand new business transfer tax of their own, a sort of GST, Grit sneaky tax. This scam is little more than a hidden tax intended to fool taxpayers". That really sums it up, does it not?
Here is another one. This is a good one from Claire Hoy in The Sudbury Star: "To find a replacement', Mr. Chretien said, 'you have to know what you have to replace. We have to know the figures and we are not privy to that information'. That is a lie. Mr. Chretien knows exactly how much money the government collects from the GST. It is no secret. The government puts out quarterly economic statements which even he can read".
I do not think there is any question. I can go on at great length, and I know the House would really like me to go on for quite a bit longer but I must give others an opportunity to participate in this debate.
Just as there is no doubt that Bill C-76 is going to pass the House today because it is the right direction and the right move for Canada, when Liberal economics and NDP funny money ideas are put before the Canadian people there is no doubt where Canadians will put their X. When Canadians have a chance to look at what is offered by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, by the Leader of the Liberal Party or by the Prime Minister, who has served this country so well for eight and a half years, there is no doubt what their vote will be. Their vote will be with me and this government to see that the progress that has been made for the last eight and a half years continues.
My friends opposite might as well vote for the reduction in those ministerial salary raises today because it is not going to hurt them one iota as they will not have the privilege of enjoying them.

The long and the short of it is that little that we have heard today is factually correct.
First, let us talk about Bill C-76. As of last count, that is what we were supposed to be debating in any case. The member across told us that this House had not been fast enough to react and to adopt this measure.
I say to the member across that I make no apologies for the fact that I have no intention to pass the bill. The bill should be defeated and not passed. In any case, the allegation, along with several others, is factually incorrect.
First, the member said the government invoked this particular provision last February and that members should be ashamed for delaying the bill this long.
Maybe he is right in terms of shame. The shame belongs to the government House leader across the way. If this bill was so urgent last February, why did the government only introduce the bill in the House on May 1, 1992? It blames the opposition because it failed to introduce its own bill.
Second, in the unlikely event that I have not convinced the hon. members yet, does the House know when the government decided to debate the bill? It was on November 16, for the first time. This is a bill that was supposed to be urgent, according the member across the way.
After debating it for a whole three hours that day the government decided to invoke closure after another three hours. It blames the opposition for that. Then the government forgot about the bill altogether, completely, and it was put on hold. On February 5, after one day of debate in committee, it invoked closure at committee and returned it to the House.

The hon. member across does not know how to invoke closure in committee. I remember when he was the chairman of the committee on the GST. Surely he remembers how he did it.
On February 12 the bill was debated another day in the House of Commons and the government moved closure again. This is where we are. All of this would be silly
February 19, 1993

even if the bill was good, but the bill is bad. Therefore the member across has no case at all.
The hon. member talked a little bit about economics. I do not know in what subject the hon. member majored but it was probably not economics. He explained deficit reduction this way. He said: "When the Liberals left power the deficit was high and we have reduced it since". The deficit was $34 billion that year and it went from $34 billion to $35 billion. According to the hon. member across the way that is a reduction.
Every year in every budget the government has announced a deficit reduction but it is still at $34 billion. How does that constitute a reduction? That is the deficit.
Let us go to the national debt, which is the accumulation of all deficits for previous years. The member says that his party, his government has not increased the national debt. Who did it then? Was it the provincial New Democrats in Ontario?

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: They are trying.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: They are trying. Is it the devil that made him do it? The national debt went from $168 billion in 1984 to $450 billion this year.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: It went there all by itself.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It went there all by itself. It is not the fault of the member across the way. Bill C-76 is one of those so-called deficit reduction bills.
I want to deal with specific clauses of the bill. What does this bill do? It does two main things. First, it imposes registration fees on lobbyists. Second, it imposes fees on student loans. I want to address these two issues in sequence.
First, on the lobbyists registration issue, it is true that some lobbyists are rich. It is true that some of the activities of lobbyists have led us all to question what they are doing. There is a committee report dealing with that right now. It is also true that there is such a thing as a tier II lobbyist. They are advocacy groups, groups of farmers, groups representing public health organizations and so on. They are also registered as lobbyists. They are called tier II lobbyists in our system.
Government Orders
I know something about the act having assisted in the drafting of the report in 1987, the bill in 1988 and the review of it right now.
They are composed of a whole variety of groups. Whether they are rich or poor no one should ever have to pay for the privilege of seeing an MP. That is wrong. It is morally wrong.
Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, our manual that dictates to us how this Parliament should operate, talks about this. It has been the authority for hundreds and hundreds of years. Let me quote from Erskine May's 20th edition.
It refers to the right to petition the Crown and Parliament. In other words, it talks about the right to make representation for what one wants, regardless of whether the group making that representation is a rich lobbyist like GCI or an organization like that, the Federation of Agriculture in my riding, or any other group.
It says:
The right of petitioning the Crown and Parliament for redress of grievances is acknowledged as a fundamental principle of the constitution. It has been uninterruptedly exercised from very early times, and has had a profound effect in determining the main forms of parliamentary procedure.
It goes on to say:
The rights of petitioners and the power of the House to deal with petitions were expressed in two resolutions of the Commons in 1669.
For 324 years people have had the right to make representation to those who they elect. It does not matter whether the fee is $1 or $1,000, no one should have to pay a fee to see me, the Prime Minister, the member across the way or anyone else. That is wrong.
Those who are advocating this say: "So what, the lobbyists are rich". Maybe some of them are. That is not the point. The point is that this institution exists for everyone and everyone should have the right to make representation to his or her member of Parliament.
I am not the only one who feels that way. The member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore agrees with me on that point. He has spoken eloquently on this issue both in the House of Commons and in committee, and he is a Conservative member.

February 19, 1993
Government Orders
There are several others who agree on that point. Any student of parliamentary procedure would understand that. If this debate was even entertained in the British House of Commons it would be thrown out as being unconstitutional. The member across the way is treating this as a joke but it is not.
On the other point if I may-

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: How about Bill C-76?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is Bill C-76. Perhaps the member across should read it.
We are talking about the imposition of fees on people for the privilege of addressing their grievances to Parliament. That is covered in Bill C-76. Perhaps the member across has not read it. That is okay. He can. He can familiarize himself with the topic and then he will know that is exactly what this bill does.
The other part of the bill concerns having fees applied to student loans. There are a number of young people who work in this Chamber for us. They are our pages. Perhaps some of them have had to borrow funds in order to obtain an education. There is nothing wrong with that.
It is always better when we do not have to borrow because we do not have to pay it back. However for those who do, why should they have a 3 per cent tax on the privilege of borrowing the funds?
If a financial institution charged a tax for the privilege of borrowing from it we as a House of Commons would outlaw it. We would call it usury. We would call it all kinds of things. We would probably invent a new article for the Criminal Code to deal with it.
No private institution would dare do that. There would be so much bad press and so much bad coverage that it would not do it.
What will a 3 per cent tax up front on student loans do?
I will have to grant this to the member across the way: He is going to obtain $23.4 million with this measure. He is going to obtain $23.4 million from the young people of Canada who are trying to obtain a post-secondary education to hopefully make a better life for themselves, reduce the incidence of unemployment and obtain technical skills. This is how we reward them, with $23.4 million worth of fees added on to their costs.
If that is not bad enough, let me talk about the other clause of the bill. In fact, $35 million will also be yielded by the provision whereby students will no longer have six months after finishing school to pay the money back. They finish school in April or May, depending on whether they are going to a community college or a university. When they leave that school with everyone else, with the summer rush, with people scrambling all over to find a job, they are in competition with everyone else and are unlikely to get a job until September when all the others go back to school and they can finally position themselves. The months that were interest-free, to allow a student when he or she gets out of school to find a job, have been removed. Now they start paying interest right away.
The member for Mississauga South says that is right. I do not know if he means that is what is contained in the bill or if he means that he approves of it. I really hope it is not the latter. I hope that he as a free-thinking member, as he is known to be, will understand that is wrong.
My colleagues and I will not stand idly by. We will not give our consent to this bill. We are going to continue to oppose it because we feel it is wrong, on both counts I raised earlier. The member across can say that we should vote for the bill. It is all wrong but there is a clause in it to reduce the Prime Minister's salary and because there is a clause in it to reduce the salary of someone who is not even competent to do his job we should approve the bill. The rationale for that is a little hard to swallow.
If the Prime Minister does not feel that he is worth his pay that is his problem. Most Canadians would agree that he is not worth what we pay him and the same goes for his ministers. If they were judged on performance their salaries would not be too big.
Let us leave that aside for the moment because they are not going to be there very much longer anyway. They are in the fifth year of their four-year mandate. Sooner or later the Prime Minister and his government will have to muster the necessary intestinal fortitude to call the election. When the government does call the election the Canadian public will judge it. They will make the judgment so that it will not be a 5 per cent pay cut that the Prime Minister will get but a 100 per cent pay cut when he is turfed out of office by the Canadian public.
February 19, 1993

We have a government across the way that has embarked on a program-and I know because I participated in the process in my own riding-called the stay in school initiative to try to convince our young people not to drop out and stay in school. What kind of conflicting message are we sending to young people when on one hand we are telling them not to quit school and on the other hand we are imposing user fees on them if they stay in school and are removing the provisions to help them stay in school?
What kind of a message is that? It is a stupid message, that is what it is, and it is wrong. I know they have a majority government today. When the time comes consideration of this bill will end. On Monday there will be a vote on it because the government has invoked closure.
I say to the members across the way: "Never mind the nonsense; vote against this bill. It does not defeat the government. That is not true. That is hog-wash. Even if it is a so-called budget bill, it does not defeat the government. It defeats the bill". It would be a heck of a slap on the face of the Minister of Finance but it should still be done.

Madam Speaker, over one year ago the government recognized Croatia as an independent state, but the government has yet to initiate diplomatic relations despite the fact that the government maintains a consulate in Zagreb.
The House will know that the consulate in Zagreb is a consulate to the embassy in Belgrade and a virtual state of war exists between Croatia and Serbia.
I call upon the minister of external relations to immediately open diplomatic relations with Croatia, to make our consulate in Zagreb an embassy, and to quit the pretence that Zagreb is really a consulate for our embassy that deals with the Republic of Yugoslavia which for all intents and purposes no longer exists.

Madam Speaker, late last year the RCMP Public Complaints Commission issued a report recommending among other matters that the Commissioner of the RCMP apologize to Kitty Nowdluk-Reynolds.
Kitty, Canadians will recall, is the young Inuk woman who was victimized twice in 1990. She suffered a vicious sexual assault and was then subjected to horribly insensitive and inhumane treatment by the Canadian justice system.
In January the commissioner apologized to Kitty for the inconsiderate and unacceptable behaviour of certain members of the RCMP. He expressed regret over their unprofessionalism and their failure to respect the basic tenets of human kindness. I thank the commissioner for his apology, but there are many other recommendations in the commission's report that need to be acted upon in order to improve the criminal justice system.
For Kitty's sake and for the sake of all victims I urge the government to implement these recommendations which deal with the special needs of persons who are victims of crime. Kitty's ordeal must never again be repeated.

February 19, 1993

UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to say a word this morning about the issue of world population and the failure of the UNCED meeting in Rio last June to address the appropriate issues there.
On December 30, 1992 Anita Gordon, media advisor to Maurice Strong, Secretary-General at the UNCED meeting in Rio who by the way is a Canadian, and co-author of the book It's a Matter of Human Survival, in discussing the failure of the earth summit at UNCED and referring to Agenda 21, the agenda for that meeting, said:
In fact, if you examine Agenda 21 carefully, you'll see that what it does is talk about our symptoms. It does not talk about our basic problem'. It talks about water quality. It talks about deforestation. It talks about loss of species. It does not deal with the fundamental problem, the thing that is sort of setting everything on fire on this planet, and that's the human species.
It does not talk about how we ourselves are expanding on the planet. It doesn't talk about overpopulation and it doesn't- certainly not -talk about overconsumption, which is the problem in the West. And, because it doesn't deal with those two basic fundamental things, it really does not attack the root of the problem.
What we need is more foreign aid directed toward education and health care.

Canada Post says that if a letter is delivered to you in error it is now your responsibility to place it in a new envelope, readdress it, put a new stamp on it and put it back in the mail.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to express my disappointment over the government decision to launch a study on how best to collect tax on prepaid funeral trust funds.
By imposing yet another tax this government has shown its lack of compassion to the seniors of Canada. As it is, people must pay the GST on all funeral costs including headstones and caskets. Surely prearranged funeral costs should be spared from any unfair taxation.
People who prepay for funerals want the peace of mind that goes along with it. By taxing these trust
deposits there is no incentive for persons to prearrange their funerals.
The government has unfairly taxed everything from books to women's hygiene products and now it is attempting to tax prearranged funerals.
I call on the government to stop its attack on our seniors who built this country. Surely our seniors have earned the right to peace of mind.

Madam Speaker, I was disappointed to learn the other day that the parliamentary committee studying the North American free trade agreement has decided to cancel a hearing in Saskatchewan.
I have a letter from Mr. Paul Brassard, co-ordinator of the Rural Life Ministry. He wrote:
The tour to Saskatchewan has been cancelled. We were missed in
April and now again. What is happening to our democratic process?
We are a part of Canada and insist that we be heard on NAFTA.
Those are the facts from Paul Brassard, co-ordinator of the Rural Life Ministry, a highly respected group in Saskatchewan.
They have the right to be heard. The people of Saskatchewan have the right to be heard on NAFTA. I insist that a parliamentary committee go to our province and let the people speak. I am not sure what the government is afraid of or what the opposition is afraid of, but these people have the right to speak.

Madam Speaker, yesterday at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa a large map of Canada was raised containing more than 200,000 signatures in support of the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture Report entitled The Ties that Bind.
The raising of that banner marks the beginning of an aggressive campaign by Canada's cultural community to raise the priority for arts and cultural activities in the context of the forthcoming federal budget.

While that is a reasonable objective, I think the higher goal is to reach out to individual Canadians at all levels across the country in a campaign to create cultural awareness and to ignite the spirit of appreciation for and participation in cultural activities.
It is with the people of our nation that the priority for culture must first be elevated if it is ultimately to be reflected in government policies and budgets. That mission is one which has long been pursued by the Canadian Conference of the Arts. It is fitting that its launch of The Ties that Bind project yesterday will hopefully prove the catalyst to such a national cultural campaign on a continuing and lasting basis.
The arts and cultural activities in Canada deserve a higher priority both among the people of Canada and with their governments.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to express my utter disdain for the Prime Minister's cruel defence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his remarks concerning sexual harassment. The Prime Minister has only added to the agony of women who live daily with the contemptible behaviour the Prime Minister has condoned by failing to demand an apology from his minister.
Let me make it perfectly clear. Sexual harassment is not a laughing matter, ever. Sexual harassment destroys people, destroys families, poisons the work environment and keeps women subservient and stigmatized. Sexual harassment is not a compliment. It is not something with which one is favoured. It is humiliating, degrading, terrifying and soul destroying.
A few dozen or a few hundred appointments do nothing to help thousands of women who are being emotionally and economically destroyed by the obscenity of harassment. It is now the Prime Minister who owes Canadian women an apology.

Columbia fishing industry is facing another tense summer over the aboriginal fishing strategy. In order to maintain any conservation measures and to prevent serious confrontation between whites and natives certain things must occur.
First, there must be consultation with all parties involved: the processors, the sports and commercial fishermen, the natives, the province and the federal government. This consultation process is being initiated by the minister this week in Vancouver.

Madam Speaker, on March 31, 1991, 500 workers lost their jobs when Abitibi's Thunder Bay mill was permanently closed. A year later 245 workers at Domtar's Red Rock mill lost their jobs when that mill reduced its operation. During the last two years hundreds more at Abitibi's provincial paper mill and other mills in Thunder Bay and area have lost their jobs as a result of downsizing.
The list goes on, with 200 workers at Canadian Pacific Forest Products now in danger of seeing their craft mill in Thunder Bay closing and yet another 100 workers at Provincial Papers as they continue to restructure.
Under the existing Unemployment Insurance Act anyone who loses his or her job and gets severance pay has to wait until the severance has run out before collecting unemployment insurance. Under that same act workers who in these cases have paid into unemployment insurance for decades are cut off from UIC after a total of two years from the date of lay-off.
In some cases family supporters who have paid into UIC for all of their work lives and who have never drawn pogey will not get one cent from this government.
February 19, 1993

I call on the government to act immediately to ensure that workers get the full UIC benefits they have paid for.

Madam Speaker, for the last 15 years World Vision Canada has encouraged teenagers from across the country to abstain from eating solid food for 30 hours in an effort to raise awareness of the issues of Third World hunger.
If we take just a moment to think of our friends from the Third World it will incite us to make that little effort which can contribute to better living for those less fortunate people. We as Canadians can do something about it. Participating in this 30-hour famine will give us a great experience of sharing.
In my riding students from the St-Alphonsus School in Chapeau and students from the Cite etudiante in Man-iwaki and elsewhere are participating in this 30-hour famine. I wish to congratulate the students and their teachers.
I urge all Canadians across Canada to take part in this worth-while effort to raise awareness of Third World hunger and to show that we care. We can only hope that our contribution can make for a brighter future for those less fortunate.
Thank you students on behalf of those who will benefit from your efforts this weekend.

With the stated defence policy of a total force concept since 1987, the Canadian Forces Reserves are an essen-

February 19, 1993

Yesterday the leader of the New Democratic Party released an economic paper outlining specific proposals for an alternative to the government's policies. The fact is the New Democratic Party was prepared to put it in writing while the Liberals are still hiding on all the major issues in this country.
Yesterday in response to the document produced by our party, the government House leader said that he was opposed to our position of abrogating NAFTA and the free trade agreement. We still do not know where the Liberals are.
When the government House leader made that statement was he aware that another 250 jobs were lost in Oshawa in the radiator plant as a direct result of that continuing free trade agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am in the process of reading the NDP economic plan.
It is good bedtime reading. It would put you to sleep.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
It is not going too badly. I am getting there.

February 19, 1993
Oral Questions
I have to say, with due respect for the leader of the NDP and my friend who just spoke, that while there is lots in there that I as a Progressive Conservative would disagree with, I commend the leader of the NDP for having the courage and the principle to bring forward a plan as opposed to the Liberals who indulge in shell games, hypocrisy and evasion of responsibility.
It happened that unfortunately the leader of the NDP brought out recommendations for example with regard to the cancellation of NAFTA on the very same day that Canadian exports jumped to $157 billion, the highest in history. Our merchandise trade balance with the United States reached $17.7 billion and trade exports to the United States are $20 billion higher today than when the free trade agreement was signed.

Madam Speaker, that is cold comfort for the 250 people who have lost their jobs in Oshawa. It is cold comfort for the two million people who line up every week in this country at food banks and the 1.5 million people who have been unemployed since this government was elected and continued that chronic unemployment.
I do not expect specious answers from the Prime Minister. We do not know whether or not he is keeping his job. That is not what Canadians are concerned about. What we want to know is how can we get Canadians back to work when our jobs are going to the United States and will go to Mexico if we continue these foolish trade policies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend asks a very key question: how do we keep and build very good jobs? The answer has to be with an economy with low inflation.
Inflation is now at 1.5 per cent, which is the lowest in 30 years in Canada. I suspect it has a lot to do with low interest rates which in 1992 averaged their lowest in 20 years.
More important than that, it has to do with increased productivity, which is up by 2.6 per cent, and the lowering of unit costs compared with the United States. In the first three quarters of 1992, our unit costs were down 6.6 per cent, which means that this combination of activity indicates very clearly that Canada has become strongly
more competitive, therefore in a position to sell more abroad and create value-added jobs at home.

Madam Speaker, I do not suppose there is too much time in Question Period to get into debate. However, I want to make one point before I ask my question.
The unit costs have dropped simply because there has been a transfer of manufacturing tax off the corporate structure and on to the backs of the Canadian people through the GST. That is why the unit costs have dropped and that is where the Canadians are paying the subsidy.
There is 11 per cent unemployment in this country. In some regions it is up to 16 per cent. Does the Prime Minister think it is good enough for the Canadian people to hear nothing from the Liberals and sophistry from the government as they attempt to plan their lives in the face of all of these promises and still have no results?
What can he possibly say in terms of specific answers for jobs for Canadians now, not pie in the sky?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of those indulging in sophistry, I cannot speak for the phoneys but I will speak for the sophists today.
To answer my hon. friend, there were some 57,000 new jobs created in December; some 45,000 new jobs created in January and it is forecast that approximately 350,000 new jobs will be created this year.
According to the OECD, employment growth for Canada in 1993-94 will be the highest of the OECD and the G-7 countries. Employment will be strong and durable, providing we keep inflation low, our unit costs low and we continue to strengthen our productivity and trade into new markets being opened by the free trade agreement and by NAFTA. That is the way jobs are created in Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to ask a question of the Prime Minister.
Yesterday, his minister of employment delivered what can be described as a disgraceful speech before the Empire Club in Toronto where he attacked once again

February 19, 1993

the unemployed and the unemployment insurance system. He said that Canada's social system is like a net that catches fish. Hardly a proper reference to the many thousands of Canadian men and women who are out of work.
In the short time the Prime Minister has left, could he not find himself a minister of employment and immigration who would put his or her energies to putting people back to work and creating training opportunities rather than undermining the unemployment insurance system which is a basic fundamental element of the labour market in this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the unemployment insurance system is precisely that: provided that its objectives are not distorted from providing for insurance against unemployment to insurance for just about anybody who chooses to leave his or her job for no reason or no provocation.
The ultimate original objectives were sound. Around 1971-72 the pattern began which has transformed unemployment insurance from something quite divergent from its original objectives.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration knows all about it. He comes from northern New Brunswick, and he is very sensitive to the questions raised by my hon. friend. He is aware of the value of these social programs to people because they impact so heavily on northern New Brunswick.
As a Canadian and as a minister, he is also aware of the greater damage that occurs when the fiscal strength of the country is drained away by abuses that should not be inflicted on ordinary Canadian taxpayers. He is in the process of trying to clean some of these up and he had hoped to count on the support of my hon. friend. Perhaps that will still be forthcoming.

Madam Speaker, I would like to raise this question with the Prime Minister. He talks about distortions in the system. What is a more damaging distortion of the system than the fact that at present there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have already exhausted their benefits and have had to go on the welfare rolls?
Oral Questions
In my own city of Winnipeg the rolls have increased by 400 per cent over the last couple of years simply because the unemployment system under this government has been undermined and has deteriorated.
Does the government know and understand that there is a very specific problem of people who want to work, who do not have benefits any longer, whose jobs are not there because the government policies have trapped them into an unemployment ghetto? When will we have a minister of employment who will begin to seriously address that issue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be interesting, apart from the criticism, to hear from a Liberal about a given plan. What are his ideas, apart from the criticism?
We have already indicated that the programs we have are good. They can be amended, they can be strengthened, consistent with the need to strengthen the fiscal framework of Canada.
My hon. friend may have noticed that in the speech by President Clinton the other night, one of the points he mentioned was that if he did not get a deficit reduction program in place of the nature he indicated, some $400 or $500 billion over the next five or six years, he was horrified by the thought that 20 cents of every tax dollar in the United States would go to service the debt. He said: "We must stop this. This would debilitate the economy of the United States if ever we got into the position of paying 20 cents on the dollar."
The day I became Prime Minister I inherited a situation where 32 cents of every dollar went to service the debt. In 1984, for every dollar of tax revenue brought in, we were spending $1.33 in services. It was an unacceptable situation. Whether my hon. friend was in government or in opposition or on the street, he knows full well that he cannot maintain this partisanship in respect of the fiscal needs of Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.

February 19, 1993
Oral Questions
Yesterday in Toronto the Minister of Employment and Immigration continued his vicious attack on the victims of unemployment instead of addressing the causes of unemployment.
In view of the unprecedented levels of high unemployment in certain regions of this country, and I name Cape Breton which has an unemployment rate of 26.4 per cent, I want to ask the Prime Minister how will these changes, these new measures assist the unemployed find meaningful work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my friend refers to the unprecedented levels of high unemployment in Canada. I think the numbers, which were indeed too high at 11 per cent last month, were 11.7 per cent under the Liberal government when they turned it over to us in 1984.
The member ought to be more selective in his use of the word unprecedented, as unemployment was substantially higher. Parenthetically it was also higher, with inflation running at 12.9 per cent and interest rates running at 22.75 per cent. All of this has been corrected as well in the structural changes we have brought about.
How are jobs created? They are created by stopping the crowding out of the private sector in regard to interest rates, in regard to public borrowing, by strengthening our inflation rate and by strengthening the fiscal capacity of this nation to generate new economic wealth, which only comes about in one way, and that is by creating real productivity gains. Anything else is a myth. This country will prosper with new wealth only if we enhance our productivity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary is also for the Prime Minister.
On Wednesday and Thursday of this week we listened attentively to the Deputy Prime Minister actually brag about his economic policy and how some day, some magical day in the future it will be much better.
If the Prime Minister is so confident, so reassured and so certain of his economic policy, why does he not put them to the real test and ask the Canadian people to make a judgment on this tired, old, incompetent government? Will the Prime Minister do that, go to the Governor General?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if he is talking about somebody being tired, I feel as young as a spring flower. I feel young and frisky, certainly compared to some people I know.
I have already told my hon. friend that the NDP and the Conservatives are ready to have an election any time, but we cannot have one until the leader of the Liberal Party fulfils his obligations and tells Canada where he stands on the GST. This is the important thing. Where does he stand on free trade?
I will conclude simply. I hate to do this on a Friday, but the last time I heard the member for Winnipeg say: "Call an election and give us a chance" was in 1988.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance claimed the Conference Board of Canada saw great job gains from the present government's policies. This month the Conference Board testified to the finance committee that its forecasts on present government policies showed 9.3 per cent still jobless four years from now. The Conference Board said it is "a pretty bleak picture".
Why is the government supporting economic policies that have these bleak results for jobs? Will it not look seriously and in a non-partisan way at the NDP jobs plan which would mean only 7.5 per cent unemployed in four years' time, lower taxes for 80 per cent of Canadians and a lower deficit?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it interesting where the hon. member gets his figures and facts from.
The Conference Board, in its report, said that in five years' time 1,651,000 new jobs would be created. That is over a five-year period. I have read the NDP-
Propaganda.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
My Liberal friend says propaganda. Actually Grimm could not write a better fairy tale than this, I will tell you that. It is unbelievable.
February 19, 1993

In any event, under the NDP's make-work projects and the plans that it has brought forward, it is forecasting just 1,600,000 jobs which is less than what the Conference Board said.
If the Conference Board says that will bring our unemployment rate down to 9 per cent and the NDP are saying the unemployment rate will come to 7.5 per cent and you are relying on the Conference Board's figures, then you had better adjust this report that was released yesterday because obviously it is wrong.

Madam Speaker, the minister is comparing different things. What he should do is look at the unemployment rate projected just this month, as I say, by the Conference Board in its presentations to the finance committee of the House of Commons in which it predicted, and I quote exactly from it: "in four years' time the unemployment rate in this country will be 9.3 per cent". This is direct from Mr. Frank, the chief economist to the Conference Board.
The projection that the New Democratic Party has in its jobs plan is 7.5 per cent, significantly lower.
Why is the government prepared to accept this kind of bleak picture for jobs in this country? Why is it not prepared to give up its Count Dracula school of economics and get with it in the 1990s?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I must say to the hon. member that we will go to the four year period if he wants. He is saying that the NDP will have the unemployment rate down to 7.5 per cent in four years if we follow religiously its economic plan. The Conference Board, which he quotes, says it will be around 9.3 per cent in four years time. The Conference Board in that same report says that under the current economic policies of the government, in four years time 1,375,000 new jobs will be created. Under the NDP plan there will be 25,000 jobs less.
The hon. member had better sit down and take another look at this report which, by the way, is so badly flawed that it is really hardly worth reading. I would suggest-

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The community of Shamattawa in northern Manitoba has been plagued by a high degree of violence related to gasoline sniffing. In this case it has an incidence of 80 per cent gasoline sniffing. Alcohol and drug abuse are major problems. Children are suffering because they do not have adequate heating and safe drinking water due to a lack of electrical service.
A cost-sharing project between Manitoba Hydro and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was to have financed the desperately needed hydro land line to Shamattawa.
Why has the Minister reneged on his part of the bargain and why has he withdrawn his support and commitment to this project?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot comment specifically on the case of the project that my hon. friend raises, but I commit to her that I will provide her with a proper response.
The member raises another point that I think is very important and this is the question of the very serious issue across this country, but particularly in Manitoba, that is being faced by aboriginal children and families.
Since August of last year the department of Indian affairs has worked with a number of groups to deal with specific problems. Since September of last year the province of Manitoba with the department of Indian affairs and the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs has set up a task force to look at all Indian child and family agencies in that province. I think that working partnership with all of the parties is going to be important to all of the aboriginal peoples in Manitoba and I hope the results can be an example to the rest of us across the country.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. Having said that they have set up a task force does not address the issue that the Minister of Indian Affairs and

Oral Questions
Northern Development is being pressured to cut $40 million from his budget by the Minister of Finance.
Having said that, how can the department begin to assume that it can assist First Nations when it is proposing to cut the aboriginal economic development program funding by 28.8 per cent, which constitutes a $20 million cut and which in turn will cost the already economically depressed and job-starved communities 8,700 jobs?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think my friend is referring at least partly to an article in yesterday's Winnipeg Free Press. I think it is important to recognize that the people of Canada through the Government of Canada have made a strong commitment to aboriginal people, not the least of which is a financial commitment to aboriginal people, not only in DIAND, health and welfare, CMHC, environment for the green plan, but in a number of other departments to ensure that the partnership the aboriginal people want to build to guarantee their participation in their future is reinforced in everything that this government does.

Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:

Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the minister for answering my question. The Prime Minister will be interested to know that I have here today a petition with 14,222 signatures. This petition was signed largely thanks to one of my constituents, Lena Cleroux, who is here in Ottawa today.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am told that the Minister of National Revenue has used this method. However, we must check the situation again with the Department of Justice to make sure that we can intervene in other ways as well and that all possible steps are taken to deal with this situation.

Madam Speaker, in response to the government's December 2 restraints imposed by the Minister of Finance, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development seems to be unilaterally attempting to apply the bulk of the budget cutbacks to the aboriginal economic development program.
The Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations has written to the Prime Minister and has analysed the effects of a proposed 28 per cent cut saying that the impact would devastate the emerging First Nations'
February 19, 1993

economies, create bankruptcies in the Indian commercial and industrial field and result in the countless loss of existing and future communities and membership.
Is the government prepared to exempt the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development's economic development work from the over-all cutbacks that have been imposed to ensure that the commitments that have been made will be honoured and the bands' efforts toward self-determination and economic selfsufficiency are enhanced?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was delighted to note earlier this week that even the New Democratic Party recognized that deficit reduction was the responsibility of all Canadians.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development shares in that responsibility as a department of government. Certainly that department, like every other, will have to go through a process that deals with its contribution to the over-all deficit reduction.
Certain programs in DIAND have already been exempted. I use the example of aboriginal housing. I can assure the hon. member that the minister and the government will review the expenditure reductions in light of being fair, making appropriate decisions and taking into account the success of CAEDS and other programs like that to enhance aboriginal investment and non-aboriginal investment in aboriginal communities.

Madam Speaker, I hope that the parliamentary secretary to the minister will have a look at the FSIN letter to the Prime Minister in which Chief Rowland Crow talks about the acknowledgement of this being the most disadvantaged and deprived group in the country and economic development being one of the most significant aspects of their future.
I want to also ask the government if under the circumstances it can do something that should not cost the government an extra penny, but gives aboriginal people through economic development a leg up. The Americans have a set-aside program for aboriginal procurements.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I just want to comment briefly, although I am sure that my colleague the Minister of Supply and Services is better able to respond to the specifics, on two things.

Second, I would say that the suggestion my colleague makes, if not specifically able to be carried out, is the type of creative approach this government has taken in the past in co-operation with aboriginal peoples and others to make sure that the best possible advantage is taken of things like government purchasing or the construction of communities and homes.
