Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. This is a sort of seasonal question, but nonetheless a serious one.
As the minister knows, the practice of gill-netting is very destructive as a method of harvesting Atlantic salmon. There is a broad consensus among most angling interests that it is a practice that should be banned in the interests of conservation.
Will the minister consider banning gill-netting in 1993 and will he and his department enforce that ban once it is established?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has a great interest in the Atlantic salmon fishery as he well might, knowing personally the tremendous qualities of that splendid beast. I am very pleased to attempt to answer his question. He is also a great advocate of conservation in the salmon fishing industry.

Oral Questions
As the hon. member knows, we had to manage the fishery under the Sparrow decision in a way that does not infringe upon food fishing activities, including fishing by aboriginals using their preferred means, unless there is a justification and conservation concerns to prevent that.
Last summer we negotiated agreements with a number of Indian bands in New Brunswick to have them voluntarily desist from the use of gill-nets. By the end of the season there was a marked decrease in the use of gill-nets. They opted into trap nets, guardian and habitat restoration programs. We are hoping to do more of that during this coming season and to reduce the problem of gill-net fishing.

Madam Speaker, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has long predicated its harvesting regulations on the Sparrow case as a legal benchmark. Yet, gill-netting is a very destructive method.
Will the Department of Fisheries and Oceans consider challenging the Sparrow case in the interests of conservation?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the solution lies in good fisheries management. It does not lie in challenging the Sparrow decision, but trying to ensure that the aboriginal fisheries strategy which provides for conservation and, we think, the needs of aboriginal peoples to try to see that strategy goes into full force and effect and is accepted by everyone in the fishing industry. That is what we are working to do. It is by agreement that you can achieve real progress, not necessarily by threats of enforcement and hundreds of thousands of cases that go to the courts.
We are proceeding in a way which we hope will get everyone's support.

Canadian farmers are being thrown off the land in record numbers while a fund set up by the Farm Credit
Corporation to help restructure them and keep them on the land is not being used. In fact, only 20 per cent of those who apply nationally and 14 per cent in Ontario have access to this fund.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:

The hon. member may think that we are not supporting them, but we have been supporting them and will continue to do so in the future.

Madam Speaker, I think the numbers really speak for themselves. Funding is one part that will keep farmers on the land but there is more to it than it. Agriculture has to be economic in Canada and the GATT agreements will be part of that. We will continue to work with farmers to provide them with a future through the safety net programs and various other programs we have brought
February 19, 1993

forward for the last number of years. We will continue to work with the agriculture programs that we have.

speechtext:

The poverty of Canadian children will yield ever increasing costs in the administration of health care, justice and social welfare and inhibits learning and
preparation for employment constituting a cost for future national productivity.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition signed by many hundreds of people from British Columbia who have noted that there is a link between violence in entertainment and desensitization to violence in our society.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition signed by members of my community in Ottawa Centre. As you know, the latest federal budget cut funding commitments for social housing in 1992 by 34 per cent, which eliminates the strong federal presence in the housing sector that guaranteed the equal access to decent and affordable housing to which Canadians are entitled.
My constituents and I ask Parliament to urge the government to restore its commitment to social housing and reinstate all programs in this sector.

Madam Speaker, I have two different petitions today. February 19, 1993

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to inform you that I wish to share my time today with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt. I will take the first 10 minutes and my colleague will conclude.
The bill before us today, Bill C-76, includes changes to the Canada Student Loans Program, a program that I have spent a considerable amount of time on during my years as an organizer within the national student movement and during my period of time as a member of Parliament.
There are a number of things I wish to say in the short period of time I have to speak. However, I would first like to put on the record some comments about the New Democratic Party's job creation paper that was released yesterday in Ottawa. It is a plan that will increase the number of jobs created in Canada over the next five years to 1.6 million, reduce the unemployment rate to 7.1 per cent, lower the deficit and bring down inflation, and it would achieve all of this without increasing taxes for low and middle income Canadians. Eighty per cent of Canadians would achieve these benefits without an increase in taxes.
I am proud of the accomplishment of my party and I will do all I can to promote this serious plan to the Canadian people. If we really want to address the employment problem in Canada we have to address education. Therefore we need a strong, adequate and fair Canada Student Loans Program to ensure that all Canadians, regardless of income, have access to education and training.
I would like to briefly quote from the NDP's job creation plan, from page 23 of the 60-page comprehensive, well-designed report. It says: "The skills and knowledge of the work force are critical to developing our economy, no less important than our country's physical and social infrastructure, investment strategies and research and development performance. By doing a better job at training and human development we will make our economy more competitive, improve employment and economic security for average Canadians and build social justice by helping reduce disparities in income and employment".
On page 24 it says: "Provincial and territorial governments have a critical responsibility to ensure that schools can do the best possible job at teaching basic skills and at preparing students for advanced education and the work force. Strategies must be developed to dramatically reduce the drop-out rate. Many of our schools' problems are linked to poverty. A full employment economic

strategy is one of the best ways the federal government can contribute to Canada's school system".
The hon. member opposite asks what that has to do with the bill in front of us. Very clearly it has a tremendous amount to do with the bill in front of us. A full employment strategy also ensures that students have an opportunity to secure jobs upon graduation, something they have no hope of doing now. The unemployment rate for youth in this country is abhorrent and something must be done about it.
I am deeply concerned about the lack of opportunity facing young people. I am even more concerned about the lack of interest this government has shown in their plight. There are few jobs, and with this one piece of legislation there is an additional financial penalty attached to being a young graduate and unemployed.
As a nation we have a much greater responsibility to Canada's young people. These young people must expect much better from this government. I am asking all members of the House to review the bill carefully, defeat Bill C-76 and get on with real financial reform in education.
The Canada Student Loans Program is a very important program. We know that from the statistics. It is well used but it could be much better used under better circumstances. Those who have problems with the bill certainly should have them addressed.
I quote from the latest annual report for the loan year 1989-90: "From the inception of the program in 1964 to July 31, 1990 approximately 1.9 million full-time students negotiated loans of $6.3 billion under the Canada Student Loans Programs".
Very impressive and obviously very important to the young people of Canada. We should know and be aware that 23 per cent of full-time university students in Canada who enrolled in degree programs received Canada student loans. We have to address the problems inherent in this system.
Government Orders
The most contentious aspect of Bill C-76 in my mind is the Canada Student Loans Program part of it. There are three aspects to it: minor housekeeping regarding forms, the repeal of the six-month, interest-free subsidy students enjoy when they graduate and changes to the cost sharing formula with provinces that have opted out, i.e. Quebec and the Northwest Territories, both of which I understand have not objected greatly to those provisions.
When fully implemented the repeal of the six-month subsidy will cost students between $30 million and $35 million a year. This is money that is being taken directly from young people who have recently graduated and have yet to find their first job.
This is a time when graduates face enormous unemployment, particularly those who are under 25 years of age. Earlier I referred briefly to the 16 per cent to 20 per cent unemployment rate for this group of people.
Even though students will not actually have to make payments until six months after graduation, the tab will be running on the full principal for an extra six months, a move that is sure to increase the number of defaults on loans. The level of default is already a serious problem with $150 million in defaults annually. Increasing the cost of student assistance will only increase defaults if fewer needy students apply which defeats the point of the Canada Student Loans Program to begin with.
Earlier this month we received petitions in the House with the names of more than 3,000 Saskatchewan students demanding the retention of the six-month study. Who are we best to listen to in this case? The government opposite that says this is necessary or the students themselves who have come and said: "We need to retain this six-month interest relief"?
The petitions signed by these students also call for the repeal of the 3 per cent tax that has been applied to them and the proposed elements of the lending for learning agenda that the government has imposed. In particular they called upon Parliament to re-evaluate and amend the Canada Student Loans Program to enhance accessibility, to guarantee 100 per cent of student loans and to improve accessibility to student loans for part-time students.

Government Orders
These matters are all very important to students. We owe it to them to consider them very carefully. When they have taken the time to review these matters in their own experience we should listen to them.
When Bill C-76 came to committee government members opposite refused to hear the testimony from students and insisted upon going directly to clause-byclause study. One member exemplified the Tory contempt for students when he cited a case where a student used her $3,000 loan to buy clothes. Both he and one of the members who is in the Chamber today urged even tougher measures to collect student debt.
The opposition at that meeting walked out and the Conservatives went through clause by clause in less than five minutes and did not listen to or pay any attention to the matters raised with them by students.
In terms of collection, I have cases in my constituency right now where Revenue Canada is insisting on collecting what it says are defaulted student loans from 20 years ago. The students in these cases are now adults and are insisting they have repaid their loans. The banks have destroyed the records of all those payments and Revenue Canada and the Secretary of State are insisting that these loans are outstanding.
The government has to do something about dealing with these particular matters. We have to change the Canada Student Loans Program. I accept that. I acknowledge it. I insist upon it. We have to change the Canada Student Loans Program. A number of reforms must be made. This bill does not do it. We have to scrap Bill C-76 and get on with bringing in a real bill that will deal with the Canada Student Loans Program.

Madam Speaker, the member referred to the New Democratic Party economic program. He will know that program calls for a minimum corporate tax of 14 per cent. He will also know, if he knows anything about things at all, that corporate profits this year are at the lowest level in Canadian history, lower than in the 1930s, and that over 50 per cent of Canadian corporations are in a loss position.
I was wondering how many jobs the member would think would be lost if we decided to impose upon losing
corporations, corporations making no profits whatsoever, a further 14 per cent tax. I suspect that the unemployment rolls would zoom beyond all comprehension. I was wondering if he would comment.
Mr. Taylor Madam Speaker, I am more than happy to comment on the question raised by the hon. member for Mississauga South. I am aware he was part of the committee studying the student loans bill that managed to go through clause by clause in five minutes and did not even hear what many of the students had to say.
The member will be aware that in the United States a minimum tax on corporations already exists. It is something we have talked about extensively in Canada for quite some time. In fact at one point his government was looking at a proposal for a minimum tax on corporations to ensure that they pay their fair share.
Despite some of the numbers the hon. member has put before us, I find extraordinary that recently the Canadian Manufacturers' Association reported that it is having one of its best years ever. Yet it is employing fewer people and is projecting further job losses to the end of 1993.
We are seeing a situation in which the corporations are benefiting at the expense of the work force in this country, primarily driven by the forces of the free trade agreement in the United States and the North American free trade agreement in Mexico.
As corporations prepare to deal with a world economy which is run on a race to the bottom philosophy, they have forgotten that in Canada we have an economy that can be built upon a basis that relates to high wage, high skilled jobs. Those are the sorts of things we in Canada have to work toward.
I am proud of the work that has been done by the New Democratic Party, my colleagues, myself included, on developing this job strategy for Canada. I hope the government will not put on its blinders, continue to call names and fantasize about what this program is all about. Read it and study it, just as the Canadian people will because they are going to have to put up with it after the next election.
February 19, 1993

Madam Speaker, in one of my jobs prior to being a member of the New Democratic Party caucus and elected by the people of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency, I worked for the national student organization in this country for four years. It fought very hard to establish ways in which students could have access to Parliament and the Canada Student Loans Program in order to talk about grants instead of loans as part of a national program.
We argued through the early 1970s that provinces did not have the capacity to fund these matters on their own.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too want to deal mainly with the student loans part of Bill C-76.
Many campuses have set up food banks for starving students. Included in those universities that have had to do so is the University of Toronto, Simon Fraser, the University of Manitoba, the University of Alberta and Dalhousie University. I would think that is a pretty good indication of the dire straits in which students are finding themselves as they try to get education at many of the universities and colleges in Canada.
Students ask for loans because they are unlikely to be able to afford to get post-secondary education unless they can find some outside financing. Gone are the days
Government Orders
when the summer job would finance a major part of the school year. Students do not take loans in order to get extra spending money. Most students do everything possible to graduate with as small a debt as possible. They do not look forward to starting a career with a $30,000 or $50,000 debt at a time when their wages are as low as they will ever be in their career.
Under the circumstances the changes to the Canada Students Loans Act appear incredible. This bill increases the qualifying definition of a full course load from 60 per cent to 80 per cent. This measure will hurt the working student the most and the working student is the person who needs the assistance the most.
Many students can only attend post-secondary institutions if they can work part time to keep themselves and their families in many cases housed, clothed and fed. Working and attending classes become almost impossible if one has to take a full program or at least 80 per cent of a full course load.
If students in this situation are having to both borrow and work to fund their education the government by this bill is indicating: "If you can't work you don't deserve to go to school. If you can't work you can't have a loan". The result in many cases is the exit from the educational process of one potential student who would be a well skilled, well educated worker in the future.
As I said earlier, most students tiy to enter their profession with as low a debt as possible.
One of the things that has made the debt less odious is the fact that at least it did not start collecting interest until you had time to be settled in a career.
When this bill is passed, the interest charges will start immediately upon the student graduating, giving no chance for the student to get settled in a career. This means an even higher debt when the individual does start to pay. These days the chances of getting a job immediately are slim. Government policies are sending our industries south. This has made jobs all the more scarce.
Speaking personally, after graduating, both of my sons spent two years before getting jobs in which they actually used their degrees. My daughter who graduated as a chef was luckier but then she could not get a student loan anyway for that particular course.

February 19, 1993
Government Orders
There is a move to pull away from the guarantee of student loans by the government, making the banks take the risk rather than the government continuing with its present guarantee. How will the banks handle this kind of situation? They will probably handle it exactly the same way as they handle increased risks in other areas, by raising interest rates or working on a floating rate.
This makes it that much more difficult for the students first to get the loan and second to pay it off when they are required to do so. Again, this increases the costs to the students and is a further incentive not to get into debt and consequently not go to school at all.
More than 7,000, and I noticed that my colleague said 3,000, post-secondary students in Saskatchewan have signed a petition urging the federal government to drop the student loans part of this bill. The government has made much to do in the last while about the value of training and the need to keep the standards and the educational levels of workers high.
Every one of the changes to the student loans part of Bill C-76 will have the effect of reducing the number of students who will be able to take advantage of post-secondary education.
Tracy Sletto, external vice-president of the University of Saskatchewan, has mentioned another problem not directly connected with this bill but still a problem, one that needs to be dealt with. Tracy Sletto has suggested that the differences in costs of education are not recognized by the student loan operation.
A third year dentistry student pays $9,660 for tuition and instruments while a third year arts student pays $2,200. Both students are allowed to borrow the same amount under the student loans program.
The students want assessments of needs of living expenses separated from the educational costs such as tuition, books and instruments. If this goes on, and Ms. Sletto goes on to point this out, eventually only students from wealthy families will be able to afford the more expensive professional colleges such as medicine and dentistry.
If students pay more, they should be able to borrow more. The financial barriers mean that some are turned away from particular colleges.
The changes in this bill are a step backward. It has been our pride in Canada to say that if anyone wanted
and qualified for post-secondary education they would have an opportunity to get it. This bill moves us closer to the old days when only rich parents' children and the few lucky scholarship winners could aspire to post-secondary education. That was not so long ago.
The government, this party, should change that. It should take a more progressive approach to attempting to get more people into the education program. Possibly it should change its name from the Progressive Conservative Party to the Regressive Conservative Party.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think it is ridiculous that we are having this debate today. This debate was really part of the budget of the Minister of Finance about a year ago when the minister laid out all the provisions of this bill. The bill is really an implementation of that budget and should have gone through a voice vote last fall. The opposition in its usual fashion has held up this bill as it has held up every other bill that was presented.
Let me give a list of the bills on which this opposition has had to take the government to closure. Bill C-32, the Canada Assistance Plan, putting a ceiling on the growth of federal contributions. Bill C-60, the federal fiscal arrangements act by streamlining the operations of government. The Budget Implementation Act of February 1991; the Debt Servicing and Reduction Account Act; Bill C-56, the Spending Control Act; Bill C-63, the Dissolutions Act; Bill C-69, the Government Expenditure Restraint 1990 Act; Bill C-93, the Budget Implementation Act that is now before committee. We were forced into time allocation on that bill last week.
On the privatization of Crown corporations, Bill C-8, the Crown corporations restructuring act; Bill C-13, the Nordion Divestiture Act; Bill C-38, the Telesat Divestiture Act. Both are acts to try to get the government out of business and put money into the till by restraining the salaries of public officials. Bill C-26, the Public Service Employment Act; Bill C-55, the pension benefits act; Bill C-76, this act. We are on closure on this act on third reading.
We had to close second reading, we had to close report stage and now we are having to close third reading. It gets crazy. Of course we have Bill C-113 that is likely to receive closure as well. It is closure, closure, closure and that is from both sides of the opposition who say that we
February 19, 1993

have to restrain spending, get at the deficit and make government more efficient. That is what we are doing.
Every time we bring forward a measure to try to get some efficiencies into the thing, to try to cut down the cost of government, to try to run things more effectively, this group claims across the countryside that they think the deficit is important. They think the debt is important. They want to increase it. They do not want to cut anything or change anything. Just leave it all the same. Yet day after day in Question Period they ask: "Why do you not spend money on this or more money on the other thing".
This a group of phoneys. They say they have a program and it is only one program of spend, spend, spend, borrow, borrow, borrow and I suppose, print, print, print. We will be like Argentina before we know it.
Let us deal with this bill for a moment. I was involved with this bill at committee. We heard from the government officials with respect to the bill. They went over what they hoped to save the taxpayer on the bill. It is not a lot of money, but there is some, as mentioned on the student loan part, getting students to pick up the interest. They do not have to pay right away but they have to pick up the interest from when they leave school. They no longer get a six month free ride. They have to pay interest on their borrowings. They do not make payments for six months but they have to pay the interest. There are some costs there and that is quite an important saving to the government. We cannot cany on with programs that are free lunches and hope to cut back the cost of government.
The bill also deals with certain fees. We have the lobbyist bill before the committee now. This bill imposes a fee that is to be set by regulation on those who are professional lobbyists.
The cost of running a lobby program is about $450,000 a year. It is only realistic that the people involved in professional lobbying ought to pay the costs of supervising the lobbying program. We expect the banks to pay the cost of supervising the banks. We expect the trade unions to pay costs when they want to be supervised. You expect airlines to pay costs for landing fees and so on. These are costs that have to be borne and there is no reason why
Government Orders
those who are in the business of earning a living by lobbying government as professionals ought not to pay for the regulation of their services.
This is another part of this bill. It cuts down the cost to government. We also of course cut down the cost to government in this bill by reducing the salaries of the Prime Minister and the ministers of the Crown. Now that is not a lot of money, but it is $80,000 or $90,000 a year and that is important when we look at the financial conditions of this country.
Let me deal with the student loan portion for a moment. The suggestion is that the students were prevented from making any representation. That is not so. However, I want to say to you, Madam Speaker, that no student organization produced one brief, made one suggestion or produced one idea as to what changes within the fiscal constraints of the government, within the terms of the budget of the government passed by this House, could be made to this bill so that we could perhaps alter the bill in committee and come back to the House with something that they would like better. Not one brief, not one suggestion and nothing in writing other than a couple of letters that said: "We would like to appear". Why would you like to appear? Set out what you would like to appear for, you have had a year. The budget has been before us for a year.
There was not one bit of paper, not one set of ideas, not one explanation, nothing. Therefore we decided in committee that since there was nothing before us, we had other things to do and we had to pass the bill, so we passed the bill.
The opposition did not like that motion and so they walked out. The opposition walked out of committee. They did not come and make proposals in committee to amend the bill. Not on your life. They did not file a single amendment in committee as to how to amend the bill. They brought forth no suggestions and so we went ahead and passed the bill. We could see nothing wrong with the bill. It did not take us long to pass it and we passed it. Of course we passed it, that was our job, that is why we were on the committee and that is what we were doing. We were looking at the legislation going through it point by point and we did. We went through it point by point and we passed the bill.

February 19, 1993
Government Orders
We did not pass one section of the bill. One section of that bill dealt with the Small Businesses Loans Act. We did not pass that section. Another bill was before the House dealing with the Small Businesses Loans Act so we did not pass one section of the bill. We just refused to pass it. Therefore, that section of the bill is no longer in the bill that is before this House.
This whole matter of saying we foreclosed them out of committee, we somehow damaged their rights to appear, we somehow refused to hear the case is specious. It is not worthy of anything. To stand in this House and suggest that somehow they were abused, that somehow they were hurt is just not so. The Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party did not stay around for the clause by clause study, they walked out. They thought: "Well, we will walk out. We are on strike. We are not going to represent Canada any longer. We are not going to stay in committee. We are going to walk out".
They then come to this House and say: "They walked out. They did not have a chance". They had the opportunity to stay there, they had the opportunity to make amendments, they had the opportunity to make suggested amendments but they did not do it, they walked out. Of course that is what they do. They walk out.

speechtext: They walked out today.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I am not supposed to comment that way but they certainly walked out. Let us go on with some of the problems we have to face as a government.
This year the provinces, the provincial power corporations and the federal government will go to the markets of the world to borrow $60 billion. After this year is over the cumulative debt of the power corporations, the provinces and the federal government will be well over $650 billion. Right now the amount of money owing by the provinces, the power corporations and the federal government to foreigners and Canadian corporations to foreigners exceeds $300 billion.
We are probably the greatest indebted country in the world and certainly per capita we are. The question is: does Italy owe more than we? Certainly not to the outside world it does not. We are terribly in debt. We are so terribly in debt that it has been expressed by many,
including the C.D. Howe Institute last week, that we are in danger of not being able to borrow more money at all.
Last September all of a sudden we could not sell our treasury bills and interest rates had to rise. They rose by a good full 2 percentage points, nearly 3 percentage points. Our treasury bills at that point had been selling for 5.5 per cent and all of a sudden they were selling for
8.5	per cent.
We blamed that on the referendum. We said that because of the dislocation of the referendum the markets had decided to forget about Canada. They would not trust us. The referendum probably had something to do with it but probably not everything because in November when the referendum was all over-there was no referendum debate in November-the same thing happened all over again. Only this time it went to 9 per cent.
Now we have been able to chisel rates back down again bit by bit but it is fragile. It is very fragile. Our financial conditions are not good. We have borrowed far more money than we can afford to pay back. We have to get our House in order and we cannot tax more. We cannot, like the New Democratic Party would have us do, put taxes on corporations that make no money. Otherwise they would go out of business. The fact is profits are far too low.
Our friend from Windsor was making a comment about Mr. Frank's statement before the finance committee concerning the Conference Board. Several people came before that committee. Most of the time the member from the New Democratic Party did not want to be there because he did not want to listen to this stuff-and he was not there and nobody represented the New Democratic Party. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak on Bill C-76, and particularly the amendment to the Canada Student Loans Act.
Unlike my colleague, who indicated a little earlier that the debate is somewhat foolish, I must suggest that this is one of the most important debates this House has seen in a long time, mainly because it focuses on education. If this House was to spend most of its time dealing with the questions of education and literacy in Canada we would not have to worry about the kind of difficulties the hon. member is referring to, whether we are dealing with the question of deficit or the question of debt.
I know and everyone in the whole world knows that if we were to focus on the question of education we would be able to help those who are educated to find jobs in a lot of ways. If they have jobs that will mean the generation of revenue and funds and the reduction of debts, and eventually it would mean the elimination of the deficit. It does not take a genius to make that direct correlation between job creation and education.
Government Orders
Everyone has said that, from social groups such as the National Anti-Poverty Organization to the Economic Council of Canada and the Conference Board. Everyone everywhere has said that in order for Canada to deal with this outstanding, incredible problem of debt and deficit we will have to focus on education and the elimination of illiteracy.
As it is the economic situation is in such a mess that it needs the attention of everyone, regardless of their political affiliation or partisanship, regardless of whether they are premier of a province, chairman of a bank or are the government at the federal level. However, we have seen a lack of co-operation, a lack of co-ordination and people shooting in different directions.
The debt and the deficit are everybody's problem. Between the provincial governments and the federal government we have borrowed from abroad, as the hon. member for Mississauga has indicated, hundreds of billions of dollars of foreign money, and that has put Canada in an extremely awkward position.
The main objective of any government is to provide services that are essential to society, essential to the community. As far as I am concerned, one of the main objectives of any government is to ensure that its people receive the education and the kind of tools they need in order to improve their lives and live in a comfortable setting.
To that extent I have always felt that the objective of our educational system should be to prepare our youth for a changing world in the field of humanities, in the field of technology and for an information-based future, as well as to enable them to become successful members of our society.
Frankly, while young people are the key to success in our society we are seeing a total failure on behalf of every level of government to address this whole question of education in order to help them to be full-fledged citizens of our country. I only have to outline the horrifying percentage of young people who do not finish their high school educations.
According to Statistics Canada more than 30 per cent of students who enrol in the primary and secondary educational system do not finish their high school educa-

Government Orders
tion and therefore they end up in low paying jobs or on social assistance programs. For that matter, they even end up in jail by committing offences that are not tolerated by our society.
For those who continue on to university the statistics, which have been repeated over and over again, show that over 50 per cent of students who enrol at the university level do not finish university, whether they are part-time students, special students or full-time students.
Not only that, but the literacy level, which is reading and writing, is very alarming. In July 1992 Statistics Canada released an outstanding report indicating that 71 per cent of youth between the ages of 16 and 24 have literacy problems. As well, and even more shocking, 56 per cent of those between the ages of 16 and 24 have mathematical or numeracy skills problems when it comes to dealing with everyday requirements.
It certainly should be a cause for alarm to the government at the federal level and all governments at the provincial level that we have an outstanding problem that needs outstanding action, and they should take notice.
To use the argument that we just do not have the money, that we are running out of money, so we are not going to spend on education is foolish. We cannot just close the tap. We cannot look at money that we are spending on education as an expenditure. We must look at money spent on education as an investment. The only way to make money is to invest money.
What is better than investing money in the future of Canada, in the youth of Canada? It does not take a genius to understand the analyses done by Employment and Immigration, Statistics Canada and independent analysts all over the country. They are telling us that by the year 2000 we are going to have a situation in which unless people have a high school diploma there will be no hope of finding a well paying job.
Never mind that. They will not even find a job. It will be a lot more difficult by the year 2000 to find a job unless they have a high school diploma. That means that we must make it a priority of society that every single person, particularly our youth, who wants to go to school can be helped to enrol in schools.
The reason I say this is that we have it doubly difficult. We have a shrinking population. The Canadian population is on the decline. We are not on the upswing of things. By the year 2010 or 2020 a lot of people will be in the upper echelons of their life, age 55 and up, and fewer people will be between the ages of 16 and 24.
We are going to see more pressure being put on those who are in the work force to produce the kind of resources and assistance that is needed to support our social programs and those who are no longer in the work force.
We know, as Statistics Canada has indicated, that by the year 2000 we will only have 1.1 million youths between the ages of 16 to 19. That puts a lot of pressure on us as a government and as a society to do everything we can to ensure that those 1.1 million students receive the kind of education they need to be prepared by the year 2000 and beyond to support all the great social programs that we have in place.
Not only that, but the pressure is on these very same students, the same youths, to pay the debt that we have incurred in the past and which is still being incurred by federal, provincial and, to a large extent, municipal governments. The pressure is on those students, and we have to do everything we can to help them out.
That is why my party and my colleagues in the Liberal Party have been pushing over the past four years to ensure that the focus of the policy and everything this government does is on youth, the economy, job creation and everything that is needed to help our youth, students and workers to continue paying for all those wonderful services we are providing.
We can no longer do the same things we did in the past. We must do things differently because we are entering into North American free trade and we just had the free trade agreement with the United States.
We have learned from the past that unless we adapt quickly to the changes in technology and to the new era of information-based equipment and technology we cannot compete. Never mind what our neighbours in Mexico, the United States or Asia are doing. We cannot compete anywhere unless we make that drastic move, and unless we make education a priority.
That is why on a number of occasions we have called on the government to embark on some sort of tangible strategic national plan concerning the questions of education and literacy.

So far we have seen nothing but report after report. The government has put on the table a number of reports but we have yet to see an action plan that takes those reports and turns them into something that can benefit the community, particularly its youth.
My party has made some tangible suggestions. The hon. member from Mississauga was asking, what do we do? We have made some suggestions, such as establishing a national apprenticeship program. I think that would work beautifully.
If members asked the community, educational institutions, university professors, the business community and those who are out there they would hear agreement. This is the best and most effective way to ensure proper results for our youth. It is one of the best ways to help our students and our youth in order to carry on and move toward the future.
We called on the government to stop the consultation process, to introduce some sort of action plan. We will continue to call on the government to stop the cuts to transfer payments when it comes to those who are the providers of education to our students.
We called on the government to stop its attacks on the educational institutions and what did we get? From 1986 until now we have seen in excess of about $4.9 billion in cuts in transfer payments to the provinces in areas such as post-secondary education. That by itself is a tremendous burden on the provincial governments and it is a tremendous burden on the universities.
What we have seen in the past is a total and major assault on youth, whether we are talking about the government taxing books and reading materials or whether we are talking about the latest attack on the UI bill and what it is doing to our youth and our workers.
Those are some of the points I would like to bring to the attention of the House and my colleague on the government side who spoke a little earlier on.

My colleagues in the New Democratic Party had the audacity to stand up in this House and talk about the interests of students and youths when we have an NDP Government of Ontario that won on the premise it was going to reduce, never mind eliminate, tuition fees. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about Bill C-76. The purpose of this omnibus bill is to implement certain measures announced in the budget tabled on February 25, 1992.1 would like to deal more specifically with the measures that affect the Canada Student Loans Act.
Education lessens the likelihood of unemployment and increases one's chances of making a better living. Since 1984 the federal government has stressed that to make Canada more productive, more competitive and to

Government Orders
enhance the quality of life of Canadians it is vitally important to have an educated, skilled and adaptable labour force.
The report Inventing Our Future: An Action Plan for Canada's Prosperity, published in October 1992 by an independent group of prominent Canadians, has confirmed the already solid consensus on the crucial role of education in becoming competitive internationally.
The government has announced its plan to update and reinforce the Canada Student Loans Program in order to continue to provide financial assistance to eligible students to pursue studies at the post-secondary level. By reducing the cost of defaults and improving the efficiency of the program it will be possible to increase assistance to needy students. In his February 1992 budget the Minister of Finance promised that the 3 per cent fee would be eliminated and limits on loans adjusted, subject to the successful completion of negotiations with financial institutions on new financing arrangements for the Canada Student Loans Program.
It should be emphasized that the program's basic objective is and will be to provide needy students with financial assistance to pursue studies at the post-secondary level. The government is intent on offering a loans program that provides subsidized loans to borrowers who are still pursuing their studies, and does so at reasonable cost and with reasonable conditions for repayment.
The negotiations are progressing. The Minister of Finance announced in his economic statement in December 1992 that the government intended to table a bill to authorize the new financial arrangements very shortly.
In addition to a new financial structure, various proposals have been prepared and communicated to the provinces. These proposals concern the program's mission, eligibility criteria and accountability with respect to spending under the program. More specifically, the proposals are a response to a host of concerns that have been raised over the years by the general public, the provinces, students and the Auditor General.
Generally speaking, these measures will do more than encourage access. They will also be more results-ori-ented by linking payment of assistance to successful completion of the individual's studies within the requisite time frame. Fair and uniform standards will be set to regulate implementation of the program across the
country, simplify evaluation of requirements, maximize resources and increase the level of assistance offered to needy students.
It was explained previously that the amendments proposed in Bill C-76 would deal with three main issues: eliminating the six-month interest-free period after graduation, as of the 1993-94 loan year; updating the alternative payment formula designed to compensate provinces choosing to opt out of the program, including an extension of the deadline for giving notice of their intention to opt out; and allowing the minister to determine which forms will be used in the program.
I will deal with each issue separately. First of all, the bill proposes to eliminate the six-month interest-free period after graduation. At the present time, the government guarantees loans made to full-time students by lending institutions and subsidizes these loans by paying interest costs while the students are at school and for six months after graduation.
After completing their studies, students must enter into a consolidated repayment agreement with their lending institutions. Borrowers must repay the principal and the interest accrued starting on the first day of the seventh month following their graduation. Depending on the total sum borrowed, repayment may extend over a period of nine and a half years.
The interest subsidy on student loans represents more than 40 per cent of the program's cost. Every year the subsidy costs Canadian taxpayers about $200 million. This is a very costly measure and a direct and substantial investment in our human resources.
During the past two years there have been recommendations that the government should completely phase out interest subsidies, even in the case of borrowers who are still pursuing their studies. The government is not proposing any thing as drastic. We will continue to pay the interest accrued on loans while borrowers are at school. Full-time students will continue to benefit as long as they are enrolled in an educational institution.
Furthermore, they will still have up to six months after graduation to negotiate repayment terms with their lending institutions. For borrowers with an average debt of $6,100 upon graduation, monthly payments will in-
February 19, 1993

crease by less than $3.50 if they decide to capitalize the interest accrued on their loans.
Less than 5 per cent of all recipients of student loans accumulate debts of more than $15,000. In fact, 85 per cent of borrowers owe less than $10,000 and 60 per cent less than $5,000. Those whose debt levels are higher are, for the most part, university students who consequently have a better chance of obtaining a full-time, well-paid job. All things considered, the financial obligations of most graduates would seem quite reasonable.
I may add that although after graduation they no longer receive an interest subsidy borrowers remain eligible for interest relief, if they are unemployed because they are unable to find a job or are ill or temporarily incapacitated. Under this interest relief program, borrowers who are unable to repay their Canada student loans because they are unemployed can ask the government, and I think this is very important, to pay the interest on their behalf for a period of up to 18 months.
Furthermore, the existing legislation is still sufficiently flexible to allow borrowers to negotiate or renegotiate with the lender the kind of repayment terms that reflect their ability to pay.
I would now like to say a few words about the proposed changes in the formula for compensatory payments to provinces that may decide to opt out of the Canada Student Loans Program.
I may add that Quebec and the Northwest Territories have already opted out of the program. They have chosen to set up their own student aid program with the money they receive under the compensatory payments formula. They will continue to receive these payments, which amounted to $87 million in 1991-92, or about 20 per cent of the cost of the program.
The present formula, which has been used since 1964, presents a real problem. It does not strictly take account of the fact that if a participating province withdraws from the program the federal government would continue to pay costs related to previously made Canadian student loans.
The proposed changes to the compensatory payments formula will ensure that the program has the financial resources to help needy Canadian students in the prov-
Govemment Orders
inces and territories and at the same time compensate provinces that establish their own student aid program.
Furthermore, the proposed amendments would require any province that intended to withdraw from the program to notify the administration in writing at least 12 months before the beginning of the loan year in which it intended to withdraw.
The third and final amendment to the act would simplify program administration. It will give us more latitude to plan and adopt changes to the form and co-ordinate changes with lenders and the provinces.
Clearly, the purpose of the proposed amendments to Bill C-76 updating the Canada Student Loans Program is to make this program better serve present and future generations in the interest of the whole country. Now that I have explained to them what the amendments in question are about, I would ask hon. members to please pass this bill which I and all Canadians believe is most appropriate.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the member's thoughtful speech and especially his concern that Canada requires more money to be spent on education and on students so that there are better opportunities to get jobs and we can compete more effectively internationally.
It is understood by the member that this is an absolute requirement. He also suggested that all Canadians should be expected to assist in resolving the financial problems of Canada. Just a short time ago his colleague indicated that the NDP in its economic proposals was not making a sensible proposal by calling for a minimum tax for corporations. As the member will know, just a few years ago 100,000 corporations in this country earning profits of $27 billion paid no tax at all.
That is largely because there are concessions made to business. For example, the business entertainment expense deduction allows three martini lunches and even the services of prostitutes to be purchased by businesses for their clients at taxpayers' expense.
How does the member justify this kind of tax policy that on the one hand allows 100,000 corporations earning profits of $27 million to get away tax free? Why should they not be obliged to share this burden of Canada's financial problems? On the other hand, in Canada we are charging income tax on scholarships earned by bright students.
Why does the Conservative government believe that lottery winnings, millions of dollars in some cases of unearned windfalls, should go tax free and yet make it tougher on students to obtain student loans and impose more strict and stringent conditions on the repayment of those loans?
Is there not a bit of inconsistency in what the member is saying? He says we need these people to go through school. We need them to improve their education for the benefit of all Canadians. We seem to give tax concessions to businesses for luncheons and prostitutes and that kind of thing. Yet we are taxing scholarships and making it tougher to get student loans.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that ideally speaking, the member is right. Everybody should pay their fair share of income tax in this country.
Also, we have to give some incentives to industries to promote their companies to provide work for people. speechtext: It was another bill.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It was another bill, but his speech on that bill had nothing to do with the bill. He almost popped out of his skin. I want to quote him for a moment. He was excited because he had some new figures on trade. He had new export figures and he said how high they were and what a tremendous increase it was. He said it was an 11 per cent increase over 1991, the largest year-over-year increase since 1984. Of course 1991 was not a great year for the Canadian economy. Though an

Government Orders
11 per cent increase may sound very good and it is quite good it probably started from a pretty low base.
The hon. member for Mississauga South knows all these figures, yet his minister did not dare put the figures on the record yesterday in spite of repeated urgings by me that he do so. I sat here and challenged the minister repeatedly in the course of his remarks.
If somebody had come into this country from outer space after listening to the minister's speech he would have thought the Canadian economy was coming up roses. You never heard anything so rosy in your life. He cited all these figures about how his policies had worked, how inflation had been wrestled to the ground, how trade was booming and how everything was just coming out the way it was all planned by the government.
The minister did not mention the 1.5 million Canadians who are out of work. He did not mention the hardship his government has put on Canadians. He criticized President Clinton because he said that he was making a huge tax grab omitting to mention the fact that this government had taken another $50 billion a year out of the Canadian economy with tax increases since it took office.
I ask the member for Mississauga South to correct me and tell me that it is at least $50 billion. Is it not $60 billion or $70 billion now? I am sure he does not know those figures. I know why he does not say them. He is ashamed of them. The government has taken all this money. For eight years it has gouged Canadians of all this money and the deficit is still at $30 billion. Talk about incompetent management. At least President Clinton promised to reduce the deficit somewhat. This government promised it but never did it. It took all the taxes but it never reduced the deficit. Talk about incompetent management.
I do not want to get waylaid on that. Unfortunately it is a side issue to the main point of this bill. However when we hear the Minister of Finance introduce a bill, ignore the provisions of the bill and talk about his handling of the economy in laudatory terms, we have to say that something is wrong with this minister. He ignores the human suffering that the policies he has forced on Canadians have brought across this country.
Unfortunately that suffering is what we want to talk about in this House. That is what we want to discuss on budget implementation measures. That is what we try to raise on these budget bills but the government does not want to listen. It wants to apply the jackboot and put closure on it. It does not want to listen to the people affected. It does not want to listen to elected representatives in this House. It just wants to have its way with the Canadian public.
I would like to quote very briefly from a speech given by Matthew Barrett, chairman and chief executive officer of the Bank of Montreal, at the annual meeting of the shareholders on January 18 of this year. The member for Mississauga South is probably a friend of Mr. Barrett. I do not know but I suspect he knows him well. I would imagine he had him appear before the finance committee when the member was chairman.
In any event, I thought a couple of quotes might be helpful to remind members of the mess we are in as a result of the government's policies. He said: "As a percentage of income Canada owes more to foreigners than any other major industrial country and, make no mistake, attracting and holding those funds means higher interest rates". Of course the Minister of Finance boasted about how low interest rates were in Canada because, as he said, they are lower than before. But they are not low in real terms. That is the real cost of borrowing to Canadians. Canadians are paying a lot of money. Even though interest rates have dropped we are paying a lot of money, a lot more than other countries are.
Mr. Barrett also said something about the level of debt owed by each Canadian. He said: "The public debt continues to grow and spread insidiously. In 1976 we owed almost $9,000 for every household in the land". By the end of 1992 it was $60,000 and over half of that $60,000 is attributable very directly to the eight years that Canadians have suffered under this government.
I cannot let the government go without turning to its friends in the NDP who have blasted around the last couple of days with this new five-year plan. They have abandoned those plans in Russia, I believe, but we have the NDP pushing them here. I would have thought it would have had the sense to abandon them too, but apparently not. These copies are hard to come by. It was just released yesterday, but when I called to get a copy this morning I could not get one. I want to thank the hon.
February 19, 1993

member for Chambly for his copy. I see it is charging for this plan. I can understand why. That is part of the deficit reduction plan for the New Democratic Party.

going to be $11 billion. The NDP had not picked up the difference between the two. Ms. McLaughlin and Mr. Langdon -
I guess he was there to help:
- repeatedly insisted that the NDP plan would reduce the federal deficit by $8 billion. I want to say also that I thought the comment at the end of this newspaper article was interesting. The vice-president of Informetrica said:
"Conservatives should be happy with the consequence," Mr. Sonnen told reporters at the NDP news conference. "This will shift people's perceptions of the NDP".

Either way Canadians get ridden with debt whenever one of these parties takes office. To hear the NDP and the Conservatives, it is the same old plaint every day: "The only reason we are in debt is because of those awful Liberals". Yet the NDP in Ontario, when it took office, had something like a $3 billion deficit after it cooked the books to increase it and then it has run it up to $10 billion or $11 billion now. It says: "Oh, it is all the Liberals' fault".

Government Orders
The Tories took over with a $38 billion deficit in the first year and they had six months to run that up higher, which they did. They stretched and spent and it went up to $38 billion. It was not at that figure in September 1984 when they took over, but they managed to get it to $38 billion and that has sort of been their benchmark ever since.
Never mind that in the 1985 budget the Tories said by this year it would be down to $15 billion or so. Forget all that. It is not. It is double that. However, they went ahead their merry way and predicted that in another two or three years the deficit would be down, but it did not go down. Perhaps the member for Mississauga South could tell us why the projections that the finance ministers gave in their budgets all proved wrong.
Mr. Speaker, I will tell you why. I will let you in on part of the secret. The government did not control expenditures the way it said it would. It cut expenditures here and there but then it increased them everywhere else. That is what it did.
No Canadian is fooled by this. We can cite all kinds of examples of government waste and extravagant expenditure. We have mentioned before how the government could have saved millions of dollars if it had cut its advertising budget. We know how much this government spends on advertising.
I suspect the NDP in Ontario does the same kind of thing now. Certainly this beautiful book of the new five-year plan is an indication of the lengths to which that party will go to spend money to convince Canadians that it is really doing something when it really is not.
There is another thing I want to mention about this document. I heard my friend speak about this and thought he should be very careful because he said this was a plan for full employment. It says it is a full-employment economic strategy. It may be but the difficulty is, and I did not see the figures mentioned in the report, that from the press reports it appears that the leader of the New Democratic Party admitted that this would take the unemployment rate from 11 per cent to 7.1 per cent in five years.
I grant that is a good start, I acknowledge that. I am delighted the NDP takes that position, even though there may be some weaknesses in the arguments and there may be problems in getting there because of some
of the other things in the report, and I could say more about that. It is a laudable aim but it is not full employment. I do not regard 7 per cent unemployment as full employment and I do not think anybody in this party does either.
The scheme needs to be reworded to say toward full employment, but unfortunately that is not what it says. I know that the members would not want to mislead the Canadian public by suggesting that if these schemes were implemented everything would come up roses, as the Minister of Finance says it is now.
We know it is not. We know the Minister of Finance is wrong. He has been wrong before and his colleague, the former Minister of Finance, was wrong every time. The jury is still out on the Minister of Finance. He claims that the measures he took in December are the reasons that everything is working out so well today. We know it is not.
The minister also says that the free trade agreement and the GST have done wonders for the Canadian economy while almost every economist in the country will acknowledge that is not the case. Indeed, there is a strong argument to be made that the economy is now recovering from the free trade agreement that the Conservative government put in place in 1989. It has taken that long. It has taken years to recover.
I am running out of time. I had so much I wanted to talk about that it is difficult to fit it in, but I wanted to talk about the approach our party has taken to economic growth.
The Prime Minister, provoked by the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca today, tried to say that the Liberals have no policy, but we do. The policy was put forward in two recent speeches by our leader, particularly in Toronto. The leader stressed the importance of economic growth to the development of our country and the fact that without growth we will not create jobs in Canada.
The aim and thrust of a new Liberal government will be to shift the focus from shrinking the economy and squeezing the economy through a tight monetary policy to one that is based on the growth of the economy to create jobs and new industries in the future. We also said that we were committed to fiscal responsibility in dealing with expenditure control, not necessarily an $8 billion reduction in the deficit. A reduction of $8 billion off $30 billion over a five-year period is not very much. I believe the figure from the five-year plan is cumulative. The
February 19, 1993

debt problem in Canada is severe and this government has made it critical.
The monetary policy must be changed to allow a much more balanced approach to growth so that we can have some inflation, if need be, and not throw everybody out of work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member, who is a great parliamentarian and historian, would probably want to say, but did not, and I thought I might do it for him, that in the 1980-84

Parliament the Liberal government introduced time allocation 25 times on 18 bills and full closure on two motions. In the 1984-88 Parliament time allocation was used 20 times on 16 bills and there were two motions of closure. That is quite less than the Liberal record.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (FISCAL MEASURES) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will answer the question directly, and then I want to comment on something the hon. member said in his remarks. I do not know what a reasonable level of inflation would be. It will not be high. However, we will not throw 500,000 people out of work in order to reduce the level of inflation from 4 per cent

Government Orders
to 1.5 per cent. That is not what we will do. That has cost the Canadian economy millions and millions of dollars.
Not only are those people not paying taxes now, and remember it is this government that induced the recession, but they are drawing unemployment insurance. Now the government is introducing measures to take them off unemployment insurance so they cannot get a cent from their government after paying premiums at exorbitant rates to this government, which has doubled and tripled the premiums. It is an absolute scandal and a disgrace. Frankly if the government had done a reasonably proper job when it took office in 1984 of doing all the things it said it was going to do it would not be in the pickle it is in today.
I want to respond to the hon. member's comments about closure. He says we co-operated to block these bills so that closure had to be applied.
Let us take a look at the legislative record of some of these bills. I think the member will find that the debates were remarkably short. For example, notice of time allocation on Bill C-110 has been given for Monday. That is the fixed link bill for the Northumberland Strait. There have been five speakers on that bill, one hour and 39 minutes of debate, and the government has given notice of time allocation. That is the kind of record this government has.
